rationale: A wins because it stays disciplined: "Airbnb wants the corporate travel budget, and it's routing the expenses through Concur and Ramp" turns the launch into a provable managed-travel story without sneaking in extra market lore. B is useful, but "Airbnb Moves Into Business Travel Tech, Targeting the Market Navan Built" imports Navan, TravelPerk, Booking.com, and a whole competitive map the update did not provide. That is the difference between a pitch a reporter can test and a smart-sounding deck slide that gets you corrected.
gaps_in_A: A leaves a possible CFO/expense-management sub-angle folded into the broader travel-channel frame; "routing the expenses through Concur and Ramp" could be its own story if the integrations have real workflow depth.
"hosts to become mini-hotels" is sharp, but it pushes the interpretation hard before Airbnb has shown how "24-hour check-in support" is staffed, verified, or costly for hosts.
gaps_in_B: "Targeting the Market Navan Built" is not in the update. Navan, TravelPerk, Booking.com for Business, and hotel corporate programs may be plausible context, but the set presents them as supplied competitive facts.

Angle 1 and angle 2 are padded siblings. "Airbnb Moves Into Business Travel Tech" and "Airbnb Plugs Into Concur and Ramp" both ride the same dashboard/billing/integration facts while pretending to be structurally separate.
"Many Won't Qualify" is unsupported. The update gives badge requirements, not host qualification rates or evidence that many hosts fail them.
"Ramp has been a fast-growing player" and "the compliance gap that blocked corporate adoption" are external claims the fact block never gave. Plausible is not the same as grounded.
